definition: Annotate means to add explanatory notes to a text.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word annotate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know annotate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The star pitcher annotates every scouting report, jotting beside each batter's name the pitch that got him out last season.
Underline stops far short of annotate — a line under a phrase says 'this matters' without saying why.
Highlight goes further than underline — color instead of a thin line — but it still adds no words; annotate tops the ladder by leaving actual explanations on the page.

To gloss a word is to add a brief definition of that single hard term and nothing more. To annotate is roomier: a note may define, but it may also question, cross-reference, or explain why a passage matters.

To footnote is to plant numbered notes and references at the page's bottom, away from the line they serve. To annotate usually means writing right beside the text, in the margins, where the explanation sits next to what it explains.

A footnote promises that chapter three will take up what the recurring rose denotes.
Annotate means to add explanatory notes to a text.

When the software team inherited a decade-old codebase, the departing engineer spent her final week annotating it: short notes above the strangest functions, saying why each odd fix exists and what breaks without it.

Annotate is more specific than 'write on' or 'mark up' because the additions must explain something — an annotation carries information about the text it sits beside, not just a stray underline or doodle.
Annotate is the working scholar's verb: notes are added to a text to explain it.

If the note merely defines one word, gloss is narrower; if you are explaining at length in your own essay rather than in the margins, you are closer to explicate, this unit's word for full-dress explanation.

The cookbook Nana left me is worth little on the shelf and everything in the kitchen.
She took forty years to annotate it, and hardly a page escaped her pencil.

Beside the pie crust she wrote 'ice the butter first'; beside a fish stew, 'your grandfather hated this — halve the garlic.' Some notes correct the book, some argue with it, and a few just remember a dinner.
A printed recipe tells you what to do; her margins tell you what actually happens when you do it.
